title: Calibrating Scientific Foundation Models with Inference-Time Stochastic Attention
claim: Methods that recover the same trend can attach very different uncertainty intervals, and only one gives calibrated, sharp coverage.
layout: Context strip on top, 2x3 grid of forecast panels, shared legend below
description: The figure is a time-series forecasting comparison. A wide black context strip across the top shows the input history, with periodic sharp dips, over about 500 time steps. Below it is a 2x3 grid of small panels, one per method: Stochastic Attention, IVON, SWAG, MultiSWAG, Contextual Dropout and HSA. Each panel overlays a red target curve and a blue prediction-mean curve over time steps 520 to 600. A light-blue shaded band marks the 95% prediction interval. Panel titles give coverage and sharpness numbers. Stochastic Attention has wide bands and 89.6% coverage. The baselines have narrow bands that miss the target dips, with coverage as low as 7.3%. A legend at the bottom explains the colors. The eye goes first to the top-left panel, which has the widest blue band.
caption: Useful uncertainty in scientific foundation models is multi-dimensional. (a) ClimaX 72-hour weather forecasting: ERA5 ground truth, model forecast, and bias. (b) Accuracy, calibration, sharpness, and cost as complementary axes of uncertainty quality. (c) Sinusoidal example: predictors recovering the same trend can attach qualitatively different uncertainty intervals to it.
abstract: Transformer-based scientific foundation models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, but current architectures give deterministic outputs and provide limited support for calibrated predictive uncertainty. We propose Stochastic Attention, a lightweight sample-average inference-time modification that randomizes attention by replacing softmax weights with normalized multinomial samples controlled by a single concentration parameter, and produces predictive ensembles without retraining. To set this parameter, we introduce a calibration objective that matches the stochastic attention output with the target, yielding an efficient univariate post-hoc tuning problem. We evaluate this mechanism on scientific foundation models for weather and time-series forecasting, as well as a regression task. Across benchmarks against baseline methods, Stochastic Attention achieves the strongest native calibration and the sharpest prediction intervals at comparable calibration, with adaptation costs nearly three orders of magnitude lower than the next-best baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/UQUH/StochasticAttention.
